questions.question: What is `ForceRetryError` and what information does it carry?
questions.answer:
`ForceRetryError` is the error Ky uses internally to trigger a retry when an `afterResponse` hook returns `ky.retry()`. It extends `KyError`. You can see it in `beforeRetry` and `beforeError` hooks and detect it with the `isForceRetryError()` type guard (`source/errors/ForceRetryError.ts:6-11`). With `ky.retry()` you can retry based on what the response contains, even when the status code is successful. The retry still respects `retry.limit` and skips the `shouldRetry` check (`source/types/ky.ts:151-205`).

**What it carries.** It stores the `ForceRetryOptions` you passed to `ky.retry()` (`source/errors/ForceRetryError.ts:11-15, 48-50`):

| Field | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | `'ForceRetryError'` | Fixed error name |
| `code` | `string \| undefined` | Your label for the retry, e.g. `'RATE_LIMIT'` |
| `customDelay` | `number \| undefined` | Delay before the retry, taken from `options.delay` |
| `customRequest` | `Request \| undefined` | A replacement `Request` for the retry, taken from `options.request` (for example, a fallback endpoint) |
| `message` | `string` | `'Forced retry'`, or `'Forced retry: <code>'` when a code is given. An empty code still counts, giving `'Forced retry: '` |
| `cause` | `Error` | Only set when `options.cause` was passed. Values that aren't `Error`s are wrapped in `NonError` |

```ts
super(
	options?.code === undefined ? 'Forced retry' : `Forced retry: ${options.code}`,
	cause ? {cause} : undefined,
);
```
(`source/errors/ForceRetryError.ts:42-46`)

When no cause is given, the error has no own `cause` property at all (`test/errors.ts:103-106`). The `cause` option exists so you can keep the error chain, for example by passing on an error caught while validating the response body (`source/core/constants.ts:101-121`).

**Validation.** The constructor throws a `TypeError` in these cases (`source/errors/ForceRetryError.ts:19-36`):
- the options are `null`
- `delay` is not a non-negative number or `Infinity`. This rules out negative values and `NaN`, which would otherwise quietly collapse the backoff in `setTimeout`.
- `code` is not a string
- `request` is not a `Request`

**Example of reading it in a hook:**
```ts
if (isForceRetryError(error)) {
	console.log(`Forced retry #${retryCount}: ${error.message}`);
	// "Forced retry #1: Forced retry: RATE_LIMIT"
}
```
(`source/core/constants.ts:251-254`)
unsupported_claims: The constructor's validation details (delay accepts non-negative number or Infinity, rejects NaN, `setTimeout` backoff collapse) are not visible in the truncated evidence
`customDelay` taken from `options.delay` and `customRequest` from `options.request` are not shown in the truncated class body
Non-Error `cause` values are wrapped in `NonError`; the evidence only shows the import
The exact `super(...)` constructor snippet at lines 42-46 is not in the evidence
Validation is stated to throw TypeError for non-string code and non-Request request; only the null-options test is shown
questions.rationale: The answer matches every key fact in the gist and adds accurate-sounding detail. However, much of the constructor, field mapping and validation is quoted from lines the truncated evidence does not show. Only the class doc comment, the message tests, the null-options TypeError, and the no-cause test are directly supported.

questions.question: What happens when a `beforeRetry` hook returns `ky.stop`?
questions.answer:
When a `beforeRetry` hook returns `ky.stop`, Ky stops retrying, skips any remaining `beforeRetry` hooks, and resolves the request with `undefined`. It does not throw an error.

**Implementation.** Ky runs the `beforeRetry` hooks one at a time in `#retryFromError`. When a hook's result is the `stop` symbol, the method returns right away, before it increments `#retryCount` or calls `#retry()` again (`source/core/Ky.ts:1202-1205`):

```ts
// If `stop` is returned from the hook, the retry process is stopped
if (hookResult === stop) {
	return;
}
```

The method's return type is `Promise<Response | void>` (`source/core/Ky.ts:1125`), so the `undefined` is passed back up as the result. By the time hooks run, Ky has already waited out the retry delay and checked the total timeout (`source/core/Ky.ts:1128-1145`). That wait still happens. Only the next request is skipped.

**Documented caveats** (`source/types/ky.ts:125-151`):
- The awaited response is `undefined`, so check it or use optional chaining before reading properties.
- Body methods such as `.json()` or `.text()` don't work with it. The docs say calling one throws a `TypeError` that explains why. I didn't find the code that throws it, so this point comes from the docs only.
- The docs generally recommend throwing an error instead. A thrown error also stops the retry and skips the remaining hooks, but it reaches the caller (`source/types/hooks.ts:206`). In the code, an error thrown by a hook is re-thrown (`source/core/Ky.ts:1173-1182`).
- The suggested use is fire-and-forget requests where the response doesn't matter, such as logging client activity.

**How it compares with other return values from the same hook:**
- A `Request` replaces the request for the retry and stops the remaining hooks from running.
- A `Response` is returned as the result without another fetch.
- `{options}` updates options, and the remaining hooks still run (`source/core/Ky.ts:1189-1209`).
unsupported_claims: That the stop path returns before #retryCount increment is shown (line 1214 after), fine; but claim that the `undefined` is simply 'passed back up as the result' to the request promise is inferred, as the caller code isn't shown
Claim that a Request return 'stops the remaining hooks' relies on the break at line 1193, which supports it, but a Response return skipping a fetch is inferred from the return
questions.rationale: The answer matches the gist: stop returns without throwing, skips remaining hooks, and resolves undefined, with the TypeError for body methods noted from docs. Claims are mostly backed by Ky.ts 1125-1216 and the ky.ts docs; only a few minor inferences, such as how undefined propagates to the caller, are not directly shown.

questions.question: What is the difference between the `timeout` and `totalTimeout` options?
questions.answer:
The two options limit different spans of time. `timeout` limits **each attempt** on its own. `totalTimeout` limits **the whole operation**, which includes every retry and the delays between them.

| | `timeout` | `totalTimeout` |
|---|---|---|
| Scope | Each attempt, applied separately to every retry. Shortcut methods such as `.json()` also use this value as a separate limit for reading the response body. | The entire operation, including retries and the delays between them. |
| Default | `10000` ms | `false` (no overall limit) |
| `false` means | No per-attempt limit | No overall limit |

(`readme.md:404-424`)

Both options accept a non-negative number of milliseconds or `false`. Anything else throws a `TypeError`. A value above 2147483647, including `Infinity`, throws a `RangeError`. Both are checked by the same `validateTimeoutOption` helper (`source/core/Ky.ts:201-213`, `source/core/Ky.ts:501-502`).

**How they work together:** for each step, Ky uses whichever is smaller: `timeout` or the time left in the `totalTimeout` budget. If no budget is left, it throws a `TimeoutError` straight away (`source/core/Ky.ts:868-877`):

```ts
const effectiveTimeout = Math.min(this.#options.timeout === false ? Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY : this.#options.timeout, remainingTotal);
```

As a result, a late attempt can get less than its full `timeout` when the overall deadline is close. The tests show that a backoff delay which runs past `totalTimeout` ends in a rejection at the deadline, and the retry is never sent (`test/resilience.ts:504-516`).

One exception from the readme: `beforeError` hooks run after an error has been produced, and `totalTimeout` does not limit them (`readme.md:422`).

The readme's example:

```js
// Each attempt gets 5s, but the whole operation must complete within 30s
await ky(url, {timeout: 5000, totalTimeout: 30_000, retry: {limit: 3, retryOnTimeout: true}}).json();
```
unsupported_claims: The `effectiveTimeout` snippet is quoted as being used "for each step", but the evidence shows it only in the body-read path (#raceBodyRead) and does not show it applied to every attempt
Claim that a late attempt gets less than its full timeout is an inference not directly shown in the evidence
questions.rationale: The answer matches the gist on every key fact: per-attempt versus overall scope, the defaults, `false` semantics, validation errors, and the body-read use of `timeout`. Nearly all of it is backed by the readme, `validateTimeoutOption`, and the tests. Two minor points are inferred rather than shown: that `#getEffectiveTimeout` applies to each step, and that late attempts get a shortened timeout.

questions.question: What does `replaceOption` do when extending an instance?
questions.answer:
`replaceOption(value)` tells `.extend()` to use your value in place of the parent's value. Normally `.extend()` deep-merges options: hooks are appended, headers are merged, search params pile up and signals are combined. A wrapped value skips that merge for the property it wraps (`readme.md:1076-1096`, `source/utils/merge.ts:31-52`).

```js
const api = ky.create({hooks: {beforeRequest: [addAuth, addTracking]}});
api.extend({hooks: {beforeRequest: [logRequest]}});                 // [addAuth, addTracking, logRequest]
api.extend({hooks: replaceOption({beforeRequest: [onlyThis]})});    // [onlyThis]
```

**How it works.** The function doesn't change the value. It wraps it in an object marked with a global symbol, `Symbol.for('ky.replaceOption')`. The global symbol means a wrapper made by a second, duplicated copy of Ky is still recognised. The wrapper also gets a `toJSON` that returns the original value (`source/utils/merge.ts:6-13, 53-61`). During merging, `getReplaceState` checks for that marker and unwraps the value (`source/utils/merge.ts:20-29`). Each kind of option then handles the replace case its own way:

- **`hooks`**: wrapping the whole `hooks` object merges it onto an empty object, so every parent hook type is dropped, not just the ones you list (`source/utils/merge.ts:451-458`). You can also wrap a single hook type, which replaces only that array (`source/utils/merge.ts:204-205`).
- **`headers`**: merged onto `{}` instead of the inherited headers (`source/utils/merge.ts:463-467`). A tests shows that a normal `.extend()` after a replace merges with the replaced set (`test/main.ts:3251-3265`).
- **`searchParams`**: the wrapped value is cloned and used as is, keeping its form (string, object, `URLSearchParams` or tuples), instead of being appended (`source/utils/merge.ts:400-416`). You can also wrap a single key's value. That key's inherited values are replaced and the other keys still merge (`source/utils/merge.ts:301-313`).
- **`context`**: replaced with a shallow copy of the new object instead of being shallow-merged. Only a wrapper around the whole `context` is supported (`source/utils/merge.ts:379-394`, `:34`).
- **`signal`**: inherited signals are cleared before yours is added. Without the wrapper, the signals are combined with `AbortSignal.any` (`source/utils/merge.ts:360-368`, `readme.md:1078`).
- **`retry` and other deep-merged objects**: the parent value isn't merged in. For `retry`, the wrapper also skips expanding a number into `{limit: n}` (`source/utils/merge.ts:431-446`).

Inside `json` (your own data), only use it where it replaces an inherited value. Ky doesn't look for wrappers anywhere else in `json`; if a wrapper there has nothing to replace, `toJSON` unwraps it when the body is serialized (`source/utils/merge.ts:34, 57-58`).
unsupported_claims: "Without the wrapper, the signals are combined with `AbortSignal.any`" is cited to lines 360-368 and readme:1078; the AbortSignal.any call is in lines 476-480, and readme 1078 only says signals are combined.

The retry claim that the wrapper skips expanding a number into `{limit: n}` is only partly shown; the code skips the expansion when isReplace, but the claim that the parent value isn't merged is inferred.
questions.rationale: The answer matches the gist: it describes the Symbol.for marker, replacement of hooks (including a single hook type), headers, searchParams and context, and gives the correct example. Nearly all claims are backed by merge.ts and the readme; a few citations are slightly off or inferred.

questions.question: What happens if I still pass the `prefixUrl` option?
questions.answer:
The request fails straight away with an error. `prefixUrl` is not quietly ignored and is not treated as `prefix`. The `Ky` constructor checks for it before doing anything else:

```ts
if (Object.hasOwn(options, 'prefixUrl')) {
	throw new Error(prefixUrlRenamedErrorMessage);
}
```
(`source/core/Ky.ts:469-471`)

The error message is defined at `source/core/Ky.ts:63`:

> The `prefixUrl` option has been renamed `prefix` in v2 and enhanced to allow slashes in input. See also the new `baseUrl` option for improved flexibility with standard URL resolution: https://github.com/sindresorhus/ky#baseurl

What this means in practice:

- **The value doesn't matter.** The check only asks whether the key is present, so `{prefixUrl: ''}` and even `{prefixUrl: undefined}` throw too. The tests confirm this (`test/prefix.ts:62-71`).
- **The input type doesn't matter.** It throws whether `input` is a string, a `URL` or a `Request` (`test/prefix.ts:73-87`).
- **It throws inside the request promise.** The tests use `t.throwsAsync`, so with `await ky(...)` you get a rejected promise.
- **Only keys set directly on the options object count.** `Object.hasOwn` doesn't look at inherited properties. In a test, an options object that inherits `prefixUrl` from its prototype but sets its own `prefix` runs fine and uses `prefix` (`test/prefix.ts:53-61`).

**To migrate:** rename the option to `prefix`. It joins the prefix and the input as plain strings, trimming the slashes where they meet (`source/core/Ky.ts:251-255`). Or switch to `baseUrl`, which resolves the URL the same way `new URL(input, baseUrl)` does. The README recommends `baseUrl` in most cases (`readme.md:1751-1758`).
unsupported_claims: The Ky constructor checks for prefixUrl "before doing anything else" - evidence shows it runs after the input type check and destructuring

Claimed the test at test/prefix.ts:53-61 shows an inherited prefixUrl with own prefix; lines are partly visible but 53-61 coverage is fine, though the claim that 'with await ky(...) you get a rejected promise' is inferred from t.throwsAsync rather than shown in the constructor code
questions.rationale: The answer matches the gist: an own-key check in the constructor throws the rename error, with the message and tests quoted accurately. Minor overstatement in "before doing anything else", since the input type check and destructuring come first, and the rejected-promise behavior is inferred from tests.

questions.question: How is the custom `parseJson` option used when reading a response?
questions.answer:
Ky always reads the body as text first and then passes that text to a single private helper, `#parseJson`. If you set `parseJson`, the helper calls your function with the text and a `{request, response}` context. If you don't, it falls back to `JSON.parse`:

```ts
#parseJson(text: string, request: Request, response: Response): unknown {
	const {parseJson} = this.#options;
	return parseJson ? parseJson(text, {request, response}) : JSON.parse(text);
}
```
(`source/core/Ky.ts:1007-1011`)

This helper is used in three places.

**1. `.json()` on the response promise** (`ky(url).json()`), at `source/core/Ky.ts:397-431`:
- Only the `json` body method goes through this path. Other methods like `.text()` and `.blob()` call the native method directly (lines 397-399).
- It reads the text with `response.text()`, then awaits `#parseJson(text, request, response)`, so your function can be async (lines 401-409).
- An empty body is a special case. If you pass a schema and there is no custom `parseJson`, Ky skips parsing and validates `undefined` instead of letting `JSON.parse('')` throw. If you do set `parseJson`, it still gets the empty string, which lets you handle empty bodies yourself (lines 407-409).
- If you passed a schema, the parsed value then goes to `validateJsonWithSchema` (lines 411-416).
- All of this runs inside `#raceWithTotalTimeout`, so a slow parser can end in a `TimeoutError` (lines 406, 427-429). Errors your parser throws are passed through unchanged, unless the user's abort signal fired, in which case the abort is processed as a request error (lines 418-425).

**2. Plain `Response` objects (for example in hooks or `await ky(url)`)**: when `parseJson` is set, `#decorateResponse` replaces `response.json` so that it also uses your parser. It also wraps `clone()`, so clones get the same `json()` instead of the native one (`source/core/Ky.ts:765-780`):

```ts
response.json = async () => this.#parseJson(await response.text(), request, response);
```

**3. Error response bodies** (`#getResponseData`, used for error data such as `HTTPError`'s `data`): the body is read with a bounded timeout. Empty text gives `undefined`, and a non-JSON content type returns the raw text. Otherwise the text is parsed with `#parseJson` under a timeout, and if parsing fails the data is just `undefined` (`source/core/Ky.ts:814-850`).

In every case the `request` passed to your parser is the one that actually produced the response, from `#getResponseRequest(response)`. After a retry, that can differ from `ky.request` (`source/core/Ky.ts:815-816`).
unsupported_claims: "Ky always reads the body as text first" is a generalization; the evidence shows it only for the .json() shortcut, the decorated response and error data
Errors your parser throws pass through unchanged is only partly shown; the evidence shows a rethrow, not that nothing else wraps them
questions.rationale: The answer matches the gist: it covers #parseJson, the .json() shortcut, #decorateResponse with its clone() wrapping, and error data parsing. Most details are backed by line-cited evidence. The "always reads as text first" claim is slightly over-general, and the evidence for the error-data path is truncated at lines 850 onward, though the cited lines still support it.

questions.question: Does ky retry a request that failed with a `TimeoutError`, and what does `retryOnTimeout` change?
questions.answer:
No. By default ky does not retry a `TimeoutError`. Setting `retry.retryOnTimeout: true` makes timeouts retriable, but only for the per-attempt timeout that fires before a response arrives. They are still subject to the usual limit, method and `shouldRetry` checks.

**How the decision is made** (`source/core/Ky.ts:688-731`, `#calculateRetryDelay`). The checks run in this order:

1. If the retry limit is used up, the error is rethrown (690-692).
2. If the request method is not in `retry.methods`, the error is rethrown (703-705).
3. If you supplied `shouldRetry`, it runs first. Returning `false` stops the retry. Returning `true` sets an override (707-722).
4. Then comes the timeout branch:

```ts
// Default timeout behavior
if (isTimeoutError(error)) {
	if (!shouldRetryOverride && !retry.retryOnTimeout) {
		throw error;
	}
	return this.#calculateDelay(retry, error);
}
```

So a `TimeoutError` is retried only if `retryOnTimeout` is true or `shouldRetry` returned `true`. If it is retried, the wait is the normal backoff from `#calculateDelay`: `retry.delay`, then jitter, capped at `backoffLimit` (`source/core/Ky.ts:665-686`).

**What `retryOnTimeout` does** (`source/types/retry.ts:121-138`):
- It defaults to `false`.
- It covers only timeouts that happen "before a response is returned".
- Timeouts while reading the response body through shortcut methods like `.json()` are never retried, because the response has already arrived.

**Interaction with `shouldRetry`:** `shouldRetry` takes precedence over `retryOnTimeout` (`source/types/retry.ts:143-152`):
- `true` forces a retry even when `retryOnTimeout` is false.
- `false` blocks the retry even when `retryOnTimeout` is true.
- `undefined` falls back to the default `retryOnTimeout` check.

One related detail: if `shouldRetry` itself is cut off by the overall `totalTimeout`, ky throws a new `TimeoutError` straight away (`source/core/Ky.ts:710-714`).
questions.rationale: All claims, including the check order, the line citations, the defaults and the shouldRetry precedence, are supported by the evidence. The answer matches the gist on the default behavior, on retryOnTimeout or shouldRetry true enabling a retry, and on the normal backoff, limit and method checks. It omits the detail that the aborted AbortController is replaced with a fresh one before the next attempt, which is a minor gap.

questions.question: What does the `data` property of `HTTPError` contain, and why does `error.response.json()` fail?
questions.answer:
`error.data` holds the error response body, already read and parsed. `error.response.json()` fails because Ky has already read that body to fill in `data`, and a fetch `Response` body can only be read once.

**What `data` contains** (`source/errors/HTTPError.ts:9`, declared as `data: T | string | undefined` at line 20):
- If the `Content-Type` is JSON, it's the parsed body. Ky uses your `parseJson` option if you set one, otherwise `JSON.parse`.
- For any other content type, it's the body as plain text.
- It's `undefined` if the body is empty, can't be read, is too large, fails to parse, or reading/parsing times out.

The code that fills it in is `#getResponseData` in `source/core/Ky.ts:814-853`:

```ts
const text = await readResponseText(response, readTimeout.milliseconds);
...
if (!text) { return undefined; }
if (!isJsonContentType(response.headers.get('content-type') ?? '')) { return text; }
...
const data = await raceWithTimeout(Promise.resolve().then(() => this.#parseJson(text, request, response)), parseTimeout.milliseconds).catch(() => undefined);
```

Limits on reading the error body:
- **Time:** reading and parsing are capped by the request `timeout`, or 10 seconds if `timeout` is disabled. They are also capped by whatever is left of `totalTimeout` (`source/core/Ky.ts:855-866`).
- **Size:** the body can be at most 10 MiB (`maxErrorResponseBodySize`, `source/core/Ky.ts:62`).
- **Different error instead:** if `maxResponseSize` is exceeded while reading the body, you get a `ResponseSizeError` instead of an `HTTPError`. If `totalTimeout` runs out, you get a `TimeoutError`.
- **Hooks:** `data` is filled in before `beforeError` hooks run, so hooks can use it.

**Why `error.response.json()` fails:** The docs say so directly (`source/errors/HTTPError.ts:11`):

> The response body is automatically consumed when populating `error.data`, so `error.response.json()` and other body methods will not work. Use `error.data` instead. The `error.response` object is still available for headers, status, etc.

So read the body from `error.data`, and use `error.response` only for things like `status` and `headers`.

Claimed Ky.ts:62 for maxErrorResponseBodySize is supported, but the "hooks can use it" is supported only by docs; no other unsupported specifics
questions.rationale: The answer closely mirrors the HTTPError docs and #getResponseData code shown in the evidence, with accurate line citations. It covers the gist's key facts (data contents, undefined cases, timeout/size bounds, body consumed so response.json() fails), and only omits the error message format, which is not asked about.}

questions.question: How does ky tell a dropped connection apart from other errors thrown by fetch?
questions.answer:
ky checks the shape of the error. It treats an error as a dropped connection only if it is a `TypeError` whose message matches one of the messages that runtimes use for network failures. That check lives in `isRawNetworkError`. When it matches, ky wraps the error in its own `NetworkError`. Any other error is passed through unchanged.

**The check** (`source/utils/is-network-error.ts:15-46`, copied from `sindresorhus/is-network-error` v1.3.2):
- The error must be an `Error` with `name === 'TypeError'` and a string `message` (lines 16-23).
- Safari 17+ uses the generic message `'Load failed'` or `'Load failed (…)'`. That only counts as a network error when the error has no stack, or when Sentry has marked it with `__sentry_captured__` (lines 27-32).
- Deno: the message starts with `'error sending request for url'` (lines 35-37).
- Chrome: `'Failed to fetch'` or `'Failed to fetch (hostname)'` (lines 40-42).
- Anything else must exactly match a known message from a specific runtime (lines 4-13):
```ts
'network error', // Chrome
'NetworkError when attempting to fetch resource.', // Firefox
'The Internet connection appears to be offline.', // Safari 16
'Network request failed', // `cross-fetch`
'fetch failed', // Undici (Node.js)
'terminated', // Undici (Node.js)
' A network error occurred.', // Bun (WebKit) - leading space is intentional
'Network connection lost', // Cloudflare Workers (fetch)
```

**Where ky uses it:**

questions.question: Which HTTP methods and status codes are retried by default, and how many times?
questions.answer:
By default Ky retries a failed request **2 times**. Only these methods are retried: **GET, PUT, HEAD, DELETE, OPTIONS, TRACE and QUERY**. Only these status codes trigger a retry: **408, 413, 429, 500, 502, 503 and 504**.

The defaults are in `source/utils/normalize.ts:17-35`:

```ts
const retryMethods: HttpMethod[] = ['get', 'put', 'head', 'delete', 'options', 'trace', 'query'];
const retryStatusCodes = [408, 413, 429, 500, 502, 503, 504];
const retryAfterStatusCodes = [413, 429, 503];

const defaultRetryOptions: InternalRetryOptions = {
	limit: 2,
	methods: retryMethods,
	statusCodes: retryStatusCodes,
	afterStatusCodes: retryAfterStatusCodes,
	...
	delay: attemptCount => 0.3 * (2 ** (attemptCount - 1)) * 1000,
	retryOnTimeout: false,
};
```

Other default behaviour:
- **POST and PATCH are not retried**, because they are not in the default method list.
- **413 needs a retry timing header.** A 413 is only retried if the response includes one, unless your `shouldRetry` returns `true` (`source/types/retry.ts:37-44`).
- **Retry timing headers.** For 413, 429 and 503 (`afterStatusCodes`), Ky uses the delay from the response's retry timing header. `maxRetryAfter` caps that delay and defaults to `Infinity` (`source/types/retry.ts:46-51`).
- **Backoff.** Otherwise the delay is exponential: 300 ms, then 600 ms, and so on, with no cap by default (`backoffLimit` is `Infinity`).
- **Timeouts are not retried by default**, because `retryOnTimeout` is `false`.

**Overriding the defaults.** Setting `retry` to a number only changes the limit (`retry = {limit: retry}`). Setting it to an object merges your values over the defaults (`source/utils/normalize.ts:37-49`).

questions.question: How can I track the progress of a large file upload, and how is the total size estimated?
questions.answer:
Pass an `onUploadProgress` callback. Ky turns the request body into a stream and calls your callback as chunks go out. Before sending, it estimates `totalBytes` from the `body` you passed. When the upload finishes, the last event reports the real number of bytes sent.

```ts
const response = await ky.post('https://example.com/upload', {
	body: largeFile,
	onUploadProgress: (progress, chunk) => {
		console.log(`${progress.percent * 100}% - ${progress.transferredBytes} of ${progress.totalBytes} bytes`);
	}
});
```
(`source/types/options.ts:335-342`)

**How it's wired up**

`streamRequest` builds a new `Request` with `duplex: 'half'`. Its body is the original body passed through `withProgress` (`source/utils/body.ts:217-242`).

It leaves the request untouched, so you get no progress events, when:
- there is no body, or the body has already been read or locked
- the request uses `keepalive` or `mode: 'no-cors'`
- a hook returned an object that isn't a real `Request` (`source/utils/body.ts:219-228`)

Uploads also need request-stream support. In Chromium they need an HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 connection. Over HTTP/1.1 the upload fails with a network error. The docs suggest retrying without progress by returning `{options: {onUploadProgress: undefined}}` from a `beforeRetry` hook (`source/types/options.ts:322`).

**How the total is estimated**

`totalBytes = getBodySize(originalBody ?? request.body) || getContentLength(request.headers)` (`source/utils/body.ts:231`). `getBodySize` (`source/utils/body.ts:29-76`) works by body type:
- **`Blob` / `File`**: `body.size`.
- **`ArrayBuffer` / typed arrays**: `byteLength`.
- **`string`**: UTF-8 encoded byte length.
- **`URLSearchParams`**: encoded length of `toString()`.
- **`FormData`**: an approximation. For each entry it adds:
  - the boundary line, using a stand-in boundary length (`usualFormBoundarySize`)
  - the `Content-Disposition` header, plus `filename` and `Content-Type` for blobs
  - the CRLFs and the value's bytes

  It then adds the closing boundary. The estimate is meant to err high, because a low estimate would make `percent` hit its ceiling part way through the upload (`source/utils/body.ts:34-56`). An empty `FormData` reports `0`.
- **Anything else, such as a `ReadableStream`**: `0`. Ky then falls back to a `content-length` header you set. Browsers drop that header, so in a browser the total stays `0` (`source/types/options.ts:327`).

**How progress is reported** (`withProgress`, `source/utils/body.ts:78-110`)
- Each event is emitted for the previous chunk, which lets the last chunk be reported in `flush`.
- `percent = transferredBytes / totalBytes`. If the total is unknown (`0`), `percent` is `0`.
- If the estimate is too low, `percent` is held at `1 - Number.EPSILON` so it never reaches 100% early, and the reported `totalBytes` is raised to at least `transferredBytes`.
- The final event always has `percent: 1` and `totalBytes` equal to the bytes actually sent.

Don't throw from the callback. A throw fails the upload stream, which surfaces as a `NetworkError` and is retried like any other network error, so your callback runs again. To cancel, use an `AbortController` signal (`source/types/options.ts:329`).

The detail that the last-chunk-delay design exists 'which lets the last chunk be reported in flush' is inferred, not stated in the evidence.

questions.question: How are headers combined when both the instance defaults and a request set them, and how do I remove an inherited header?
questions.answer:
Instance headers and request headers are merged key by key. Header names are lowercased, and when the same header appears in both, the later source (the request or the `.extend()` call) wins. To remove an inherited header, set it to `undefined`.

**How merging works**

At the top level of the options, each `headers` source is merged into the headers collected so far (`source/utils/merge.ts:463-468`):

```ts
const {value: headerValue, isReplace} = getReplaceState((source as any).headers);
headers = mergeHeaderContainers(isReplace ? {} : headers, headerValue as KyHeadersInit);
```

`mergeHeaderContainers` turns both sources into plain objects. It then writes each entry into a `Map` keyed by the lowercased name, base headers first and new headers second. So `Authorization` and `authorization` count as the same header, and the later value replaces the earlier one (`source/utils/merge.ts:188-196`). You can pass headers as a `Headers` instance or a plain object. Either way, the merged result is a plain object with lowercase keys (`source/types/options.ts:465`).

If you wrap the new headers in `replaceOption(...)`, the merge starts from `{}`. That drops all inherited headers instead of merging with them (line 465 above).

**Removing an inherited header**

Pass the header with the value `undefined`. During merging, `undefined` is kept as a deletion marker, so it can also remove a header that came from a `Request` input when the request is built (`source/utils/merge.ts:186-187`). The docs give this example (`source/types/options.ts:467-497`):

```ts
const original = ky.create({headers: {rainbow: 'rainbow', unicorn: 'unicorn'}});
const extended = original.extend({headers: {rainbow: undefined}});
// in a beforeRequest hook: request.headers.has('rainbow') → false, has('unicorn') → true
```

A `Headers` instance can't store a real `undefined`. In that case only, the string `'undefined'` counts as a deletion (`source/utils/merge.ts:169-181`). In a plain object, `'undefined'` is just an ordinary string value.

The only soft spot is the request/.extend() framing of the sources, which is implied rather than shown. It covers all key facts in the gist.

questions.question: How are query string parameters added to the request URL when the URL already has some?
questions.answer:
The `searchParams` option is **merged into** the query string already on the URL. Nothing is replaced by default: new entries are appended after the existing ones, so a repeated key ends up in the URL twice.

**Where it happens.** Ky first builds the `Request` from the input. If `searchParams` is set, it parses the request URL, applies the parameters to it, and rebuilds the `Request` only if the URL actually changed (`source/core/Ky.ts:544-554`):

```ts
const url = new URL(this.request.url);
applySearchParameters(url, searchParams);
if (url.href !== this.request.url) { /* recreate Request with new url */ }
```

**How `applySearchParameters` merges** (`source/core/Ky.ts:279-309`) depends on what type of value you pass:

- **String:** a leading `?` is stripped. The rest is joined to the existing query with `&`, or becomes the query if there wasn't one. An empty string changes nothing.
  ```ts
  url.search = url.search ? `${url.search}&${stringSearchParameters}` : `?${stringSearchParameters}`;
  ```
- **Plain object:** each entry is added with `url.searchParams.append(key, value)`. A value of `undefined` works differently: it **removes** that key from the input URL.
- **`URLSearchParams` or an array of key/value pairs:** it is turned into a `URLSearchParams` and each pair is appended.

**Removing keys first.** Before anything is appended, any keys that were marked as deleted while options were being merged (for example through `ky.extend`) are removed from the input URL. That way, later entries can add those keys back on purpose (`source/core/Ky.ts:281-288`).

**Avoiding needless rewrites.** Keys are deleted only if they are actually present (`source/core/Ky.ts:272-277`). The comment there explains why: `URLSearchParams#delete()` re-serializes the whole query even when the key is missing, which could turn an untouched `%20` into `+`.

The option's own documentation agrees: "Setting this will merge with any existing search parameters in the input URL" (`source/types/options.ts`).

questions.question: Can a hook skip the network entirely and return a canned response instead?
questions.answer:
Yes. A `beforeRequest` hook that returns a `Response` stops Ky from making any HTTP request, and that response is used as the result. The hook docs say so directly (`source/types/hooks.ts:149`):

> It can also return a `Response` to completely avoid making an HTTP request, in which case remaining `beforeRequest` hooks are skipped. This can be used to mock a request, check an internal cache, etc.

Returning a `Request` works differently: it only replaces the outgoing request, and the remaining hooks still run.

**How it works** (`source/core/Ky.ts:590-598`):

```ts
const beforeRequestResponse = await this.#runBeforeRequestHooks();
...
let response = beforeRequestResponse ?? await this.#retry();
```

`#retry()` is the path that eventually calls `#fetch()`, which invokes the `fetch` option (`source/core/Ky.ts:1218-1247`). When a hook supplies a response, that whole path is skipped.

**What still applies to a canned response:**
- **`afterResponse` hooks** still run on it (`source/core/Ky.ts:612`).
- **Download progress:** response decoration and `onDownloadProgress` streaming still apply (`source/core/Ky.ts:649-662`).
- **No retries on a failing status:** if your canned response has an error status (and `throwHttpErrors` applies), Ky throws an `HTTPError` right away instead of retrying. Hook responses are tracked in `#hookResponses` and "used as-is, so a failing status throws instead of being retried" (`source/core/Ky.ts:452-453`, `606-607`, `638-640`).

**`beforeRetry` hooks can do this too.** Their return type includes `Response` (`source/types/hooks.ts:77`), so a retry can also be answered without the network. The same throw-instead-of-retry rule applies to those responses.

A minimal mock:

```ts
ky.extend({hooks: {beforeRequest: [() => new Response(JSON.stringify({ok: true}))]}});
```

Claim that a `beforeRetry` response follows the same throw-instead-of-retry rule is supported only by the comment, not the code path
questions.rationale: The answer is well supported by the hook docs at hooks.ts:149, the `#run` code at Ky.ts:590-598, and the `#hookResponses` comment and `responseFromHook` throw at 606-640. It covers all key facts in the gist, including that a returned Request replaces the outgoing one and the failing-status behavior. questions.question: How is the final request URL built when an instance has both a path prefix and a base URL?
questions.answer:
The URL is built in two steps, both in `resolveInput`: first the `prefix` is joined to the input string, then the joined string is resolved against `baseUrl` (`source/core/Ky.ts:245-270`).

**1. Join with `prefix` (simple string concatenation).** Trailing slashes are trimmed from the prefix and leading slashes from the input. The two are then joined with exactly one `/`:

```ts
if (prefix) {
	const normalizedPrefix = prefix.replace(/\/+$/, '');
	const normalizedInput = input.replace(/^\/+/, '');
	input = `${normalizedPrefix}/${normalizedInput}`;
}
```

This means a leading slash on the input is effectively ignored. With `prefix: '/api/'`, both `'users'` and `'/users'` become `/api/users` (`source/types/options.ts:158-175`).

**2. Resolve against `baseUrl` (standard URL resolution).** The joined string is checked first:
- If it looks like `http:` or `https:` without `//` after it, a `TypeError` is thrown.
- If it has no scheme (it's relative), it is resolved with `new URL(input, new Request(baseUrl).url)`. Wrapping `baseUrl` in a `Request` means a relative `baseUrl` is first resolved against the environment's base URL.
- If it is already absolute (it has a scheme), `baseUrl` is skipped.

```ts
if (!isAbsoluteInput(normalizedInput)) {
	return new URL(input, (new Request(baseUrl)).url);
}
```
(`source/core/Ky.ts:257-269`)

**What this means in practice:**
- Since the prefix is applied first, normal URL rules then apply to the combined string. If the prefix starts with `/` (for example `prefix: '/v1'`), the result is origin-relative: `/v1/users` resolves against the origin of `baseUrl`, so any path in `baseUrl` is replaced.
- If the prefix has no leading slash (`prefix: 'v1'`) and `baseUrl` ends with `/` (`'https://x.com/api/'`), you get `https://x.com/api/v1/users`.
- The docs recommend a trailing slash on a `baseUrl` that has a path. Without it, page-relative inputs replace the last path segment instead of adding to it (`source/types/options.ts:136`).
- An absolute prefix (for example `https://other.com`) produces an absolute URL, so `baseUrl` is ignored.
- Both steps only apply when the input is a string. `URL` and `Request` inputs are passed through unchanged (`source/core/Ky.ts:247-249`).

The old `prefixUrl` option was renamed to `prefix` in v2, and using the old name produces an error (`source/core/Ky.ts:63`).

Claim that an absolute prefix produces an absolute URL so baseUrl is ignored is inferred, not explicitly shown

questions.question: How do I use ky's XML shortcut method to parse a response into an object?
questions.answer:
Ky has no XML shortcut method. The response promise type lists every shortcut it adds, and these are all of them: `arrayBuffer`, `blob`, `formData`, `bytes`, `json` and `text` (`source/types/ResponsePromise.ts:9-71`). A test of the `Accept` headers that Ky sets for each shortcut covers the same list, with no XML entry (`test/response-consumption.ts:253-261`).

To get an object from an XML response, use `.text()` and pass the string to an XML parser of your choice. Ky doesn't include one, so that part is up to you:

```ts
const xmlString = await ky('https://example.com/feed.xml').text();
// then parse xmlString with your own XML parser
```

Like the other shortcuts, `.text()` throws an `HTTPError` if the status is outside 200–299. When you call it this way, Ky sets an `Accept` header that matches the method, which is `text/*` for `.text()` (`source/types/ResponsePromise.ts:2`, `test/response-consumption.ts:255`). If your server expects something like `application/xml`, set the `Accept` header yourself.
